before.title: Cam/Crank Angle Sensor (CAS) O-ring oil leak on 1.8L engines
before.description: On 1.8L BP engines, the Cam Angle Sensor (commonly called the CAS) mounts at the rear of the cylinder head, engaging the camshaft, and is sealed to the head by a single rubber O-ring. With age and heat cycling the O-ring hardens and shrinks, letting oil weep out of the back of the head. This is widely cited as the single most common oil-leak source on NA/NB Miatas; it typically fails before the valve-cover gasket. The oil runs down onto the nearby heater hoses (which it can rot) and the bellhousing. It is a nuisance leak rather than a failure, but a badly heat-soaked or oil-fouled CAS can also contribute to intermittent driveability faults.
before.solution: Remove the CAS, discard the old O-ring, and install a fresh O-ring (a Viton -222 size is commonly used) lightly lubricated with clean oil; reindex the CAS to its factory alignment on reinstall so ignition timing is preserved. The part is a few dollars; most owners do it themselves. A shop visit is inexpensive. If a heat-soaked sensor is causing driveability faults, replace the CAS unit itself.
symptoms: Oil weep/drip at the rear of the cylinder head
Oil-soaked heater hoses near the firewall
Burning oil smell
Occasional heat-soak stall or hard restart when hot (severe cases)

before.title: Convertible soft-top plastic rear window cracking, hazing, and zipper tear-out
before.description: NA and most early NB tops use a flexible plastic (vinyl) rear window, on many NA tops joined to the top with a zipper so the window can be lowered. With UV exposure and age the plastic yellows, hazes to near-opaque, and cracks (often starting at corners or the zipper seam); the zipper stitching tears out where the window meets the top. This is a near-universal age issue on unrestored cars and badly hurts rear visibility. A glass rear window with defroster was optional/standard on some later NB tops and does not haze, but zipper-window NA tops are the common case in this era.
before.solution: Options scale with budget: DIY replace just the vinyl window panel for the lowest cost; have an upholstery shop transplant a new rear window (~$200-300 typical); or replace the entire soft top with a modern top that has a glass window and defroster. Note that aftermarket replacement windows use a non-standard zipper that will not mesh with the original Mazda zipper, so the original zipper often must be transferred to the new panel.
symptoms: Cloudy, yellowed, or opaque rear window
Cracks or splits in the plastic window
Window separating/tearing from the top at the zipper seam
Poor rearward visibility

before.title: Fuel filler pipe non-return valve sticking / fuel spit-back (1999 NB - NHTSA recall 00V032000)
before.description: NHTSA recall campaign 00V032000 covered approximately 22,000 1999 MX-5 Miatas built November 1997 to November 1998. Insufficient clearance between the fuel filler pipe's non-return (check) valve case and shutter, combined with fuel-hose material properties, could cause the valve to stick. This produced a 'hard to refuel' condition and, in some cases, fuel spit-back at the nozzle during fill-up, a fire/burn hazard. Mazda dealers replaced the non-return valve with a modified valve free of charge, with owner notification beginning April 2000. On surviving cars the original service may or may not have been performed.
before.solution: Verify by VIN through NHTSA/Mazda whether recall 00V032000 was completed; the corrective valve replacement was performed free by dealers. On unremedied cars, replace the fuel filler pipe / non-return valve with the updated part. Symptoms of a sticking valve (nozzle clicking off, fuel splashing back) warrant filler-pipe inspection.
symptoms: Very slow refueling / pump nozzle repeatedly clicking off
Fuel spitting back out of the filler neck when fueling
Fuel smell around the filler area

before.title: Overdue timing belt / water pump service (age-related, both engines)
before.description: Both the 1.6L B6 and 1.8L BP are belt-driven and Mazda specifies timing-belt replacement at 60,000 miles. On 25-35 year-old cars, belts frequently fail on age/dry-rot rather than mileage. The engines are non-interference, so a snapped belt will not bend valves, but it will strand the car. The water pump is driven behind the timing belt and commonly weeps or fails in the same 70k-170k window, so it is standard practice to replace the pump, tensioner, and seals while the belt is off since ~90% of the labor overlaps.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt on a strict time/mileage interval (every ~60k miles or when age/condition warrants) and do the water pump, tensioner spring, idler, front crank/cam seals, and accessory belts at the same time. Verify cam and crank timing marks on reassembly. DIY kits are affordable; shop labor is moderate.
symptoms: Engine cranks but will not start (belt failed)
Coolant weeping from the timing cover / under the crank pulley (water pump)
Ticking or squeal from the timing cover
Overheating from failed water pump
Cracked, glazed, or contaminated timing belt on inspection

before.title: Rocker panel and front frame-rail rust (rear of rockers / behind front wheels)
before.description: NA and NB Miatas are prone to structural rust in two well-known areas: the rear ends of the rocker panels (sills) and the front frame rails behind the front wheels. Road water enters through wheel-arch pinch welds and body seams and collects inside the double-layer sheet metal, rotting it from the inside out even when exterior paint looks fine. NB (1999+) frame rails are double-layer ('tinfoil sandwich') and rust worse than the single-layer NA rails. Salt-belt/winter cars are worst, but even garage-kept examples show rear-rocker rot. Because the rockers are structural on these unibody roadsters, advanced rot compromises chassis rigidity and safety.
before.solution: Inspect carefully during purchase (probe the rear rockers and frame rails, don't just look). Small surface rust can be treated and sealed. Perforated rockers/frame rails require cutting out the rot and welding in replacement panels or reproduction rocker/rail sections (OEM NA single-layer rails preferred over NB double-layer). Add drain holes and cavity wax as prevention. Budget varies widely by severity and per side.
symptoms: Bubbling paint at the rear of the rocker panels
Flaking/perforated metal behind the front tires
Rust flakes visible in the sill drain holes
Soft/crunchy metal when probed at rockers or frame rails
Reduced chassis rigidity / cowl shake

before.title: Short-nose crankshaft / keyway failure on 1990-early 1991 1.6 ("the Miata crank problem")
before.description: The earliest 1.6L B6 cars (all 1990 and 1991 up to VIN JM1NA...209446) use a 'short-nose' crankshaft. The crank pulley/timing sprocket is retained by a single bolt and a Woodruff key in a shallow keyway. Over time, and especially after a timing-belt/front-seal service where the pulley bolt and cam sprocket are removed and improperly reassembled (the key seated wrong, or the bolt not torqued to spec), the bolt loses clamp load. The pulley then walks on the crank snout, wallowing out the keyway and shearing the key. Left unaddressed this destroys the crankshaft nose. 1992+ cars and 1991 cars from VIN 209447 use a revised long-nose crank (identifiable by an 8-slot vs 4-slot pulley) and are not affected.
before.solution: On affected 1990/early-91 cars, avoid removing the crank pulley bolt and cam sprocket during routine timing-belt service unless necessary. If servicing, replace the key correctly so it seats fully, use a new grade bolt, apply thread locker, and torque to spec (approx 80-87 ft-lb, then verify no pulley wobble). Many owners upgrade to an aftermarket crank bolt/washer kit. A wallowed keyway or damaged crank nose requires crankshaft replacement (engine-out or major teardown).
symptoms: Knocking or clacking from the front of the engine
Timing marks out of alignment / ignition timing wandering
Loose or wobbling crank pulley
Sheared or protruding Woodruff key
Timing belt jumping or coming off
No-start after a timing/accessory belt job

before.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor Failure (NB)
before.description: The NB Miata (1999-2005) crankshaft position sensor (CPS) is a known failure point. The sensor deteriorates from engine heat, causing intermittent stalling, no-start conditions, and random misfires. Failure is often heat-related - the car runs fine when cold but stalls or dies after reaching operating temperature.
before.solution: Replace crankshaft position sensor with OEM Mazda unit (N3A1-18-221A). Aftermarket sensors (Delphi, Dorman) have higher failure rates on this application. The sensor is located on the rear of the engine block near the flywheel.
symptoms: Engine stalls when hot, restarts after cooling down
Intermittent no-start condition (cranks but does not fire)
Random misfires and rough running at operating temperature

before.title: Differential Whine (ND)
before.description: The ND Miata (2016+) rear differential produces a noticeable whine or hum at highway speeds (50-70 mph) under light load. The noise is gear mesh related and varies with speed and throttle position. While not typically indicative of imminent failure, the noise is audible in the cabin due to the Miata's minimal sound insulation. More common on early ND production.
before.solution: Change differential fluid to a high-quality 75W-90 GL-5 synthetic with limited slip additive. If noise is excessive, Mazda may replace the ring and pinion under warranty. Adding friction modifier to the diff fluid can reduce noise and improve limited-slip behavior.
symptoms: Humming or whining noise from rear at highway speed
Noise varies with speed (not RPM dependent)
Louder under light throttle / deceleration
No vibration - purely audible noise

before.title: Timing Belt and Water Pump Failure (NA 1.6L/1.8L)
before.description: Both the 1.6L B6 and 1.8L BP engines in the NA Miata are interference engines that require timing belt replacement every 60,000 miles. A broken timing belt causes pistons to strike valves, resulting in bent valves and potentially damaged pistons — often totaling the engine. The water pump, driven by the timing belt, frequently leaks around the same interval and should be replaced proactively.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt, water pump, front crank seal, cam seals, tensioner spring, and idler pulley as a complete kit every 60,000 miles. Quality kits from Gates or Continental are available for $80-$150. This is a popular DIY job (4-6 hours) with excellent online guides. Do not skip or delay this service — engine replacement after belt failure costs $1,500-$3,000.
symptoms: High mileage since last belt change
Squealing from timing belt area
Coolant leak from water pump weep hole
Visible cracking on timing belt (if inspected)
Engine suddenly dies and will not restart (if belt breaks)

before.title: Radiator Coolant Overflow and Cracked Upper Tank (NB)
before.description: NB Miata radiators are prone to failure at the plastic upper tank where it crimps onto the aluminum core. The plastic becomes brittle with age and heat cycling, developing hairline cracks that leak coolant under pressure. This can lead to sudden coolant loss and overheating, especially in spirited driving or hot weather. The OEM radiator typically fails between 80,000-120,000 miles.
before.solution: Replace the radiator with a full-aluminum aftermarket unit (Koyo, Mishimoto, CSF) for permanent reliability improvement, or use an OEM-style replacement. Replace the radiator cap and inspect all hoses. A thermostat replacement is recommended at the same time. Budget 1-2 hours for the swap. An aluminum radiator costs $150-$250 and eliminates the plastic tank failure point.
symptoms: Coolant drip from front of radiator
Coolant overflow tank level dropping
Overheating in traffic or spirited driving
White residue on radiator top tank
Sweet coolant smell after driving

before.title: Electric Power Steering (EPS) Failure and Warning Light (NC)
before.description: The NC Miata uses an electric power steering system that can fail due to a faulty steering angle sensor, EPS control module, or motor. When the system fails, the EPS warning light illuminates and power assist is lost, making the steering very heavy at low speeds. While the car remains drivable (it is manual rack-and-pinion underneath), parking and tight maneuvers become difficult.
before.solution: Diagnose with a Mazda scan tool to identify the specific failed component (sensor, module, or motor). The steering angle sensor is the most common failure and can be recalibrated or replaced relatively affordably. If the EPS motor or control module has failed, replacement costs are higher. Some owners have had success with used EPS units from junkyards ($200-$400).
symptoms: EPS warning light on dashboard
Sudden loss of power steering assist
Heavy steering at low speed
Intermittent power steering assist
Steering assist returns after restart

before.title: Mazda Connect Infotainment USB and Bluetooth Connectivity Issues (ND)
before.description: The ND Miata's Mazda Connect infotainment system is plagued by USB connectivity drops, Bluetooth pairing failures, and occasional system freezes. USB-connected phones may disconnect repeatedly, and Bluetooth audio can cut out or develop significant delay. The 7-inch screen can freeze requiring a system reset. Mazda has issued multiple software updates but the issues persist for many owners across model years.
before.solution: Update the Mazda Connect firmware to the latest version (available for free download from Mazda's website). Try different USB cables (use short, high-quality cables). Delete and re-pair Bluetooth devices. For persistent freezes, perform a master reset by pressing and holding the NAV, MUTE, and BACK buttons simultaneously. Some owners report improvement after replacing the USB hub module.
symptoms: USB phone connection drops repeatedly
Bluetooth audio cuts out
Infotainment screen freezes
CarPlay/Android Auto disconnects
System slow to boot on startup

before.title: Rear Main Seal Oil Leak
before.description: All generations of Miata (NA through NC) are prone to rear main seal leaks as the engine ages. Oil seeps from the crankshaft rear seal, dripping onto the clutch housing and eventually contaminating the clutch disc. High mileage engines and infrequent oil changes accelerate seal deterioration. This is a labor-intensive repair as the transmission must be removed.
before.solution: Replace rear main crankshaft seal. Since the transmission must be removed, replace the clutch, throwout bearing, and pilot bearing at the same time if they are worn. Clean bell housing thoroughly to remove oil contamination.
symptoms: Oil dripping from bell housing area (bottom of engine/transmission junction)
Oil smell when parked
Clutch slipping if oil contaminates clutch disc
Low oil level between changes

before.title: Short Nose Crank Keyway Failure (NA 1.6L)
before.description: Early NA Miatas (1990-1993) with the 1.6L B6ZE engine have a shorter crankshaft snout that is prone to keyway wallowing. The crankshaft pulley bolt loosens over time, causing the Woodruff key to shear and the pulley to spin freely on the crankshaft. This leads to loss of timing belt synchronization and potential engine damage. A well-known and feared issue in the NA Miata community.
before.solution: Install the "long nose crank" (LNC) upgrade using the 1994+ crankshaft pulley and longer bolt (B6S8-11-401A with bolt B366-11-406). This provides more clamping surface area. Torque to 116 ft-lbs with medium-strength thread locker. Some owners also use aftermarket eccentric keyed pulleys (Flyin Miata, Boundary Engineering).
symptoms: Rattling or knocking noise from front of engine
Timing belt slips causing engine to run rough or stall
Crankshaft pulley bolt found loose
Engine suddenly dies and will not restart (key sheared)

before.title: Soft Top Wear and Rear Window Delamination
before.description: Miata soft tops deteriorate over time from UV exposure, flexing during operation, and age. Vinyl tops develop cracks and tears, cloth tops fade and shrink. The rear plastic window (NA/NB) or glass window (NC/ND) can delaminate from the top material, causing water leaks and reduced visibility. Expected soft top life is 7-10 years with proper care.
before.solution: Replace soft top assembly. OEM replacement is available but aftermarket options (Robbins, TwinTop) offer better materials at lower cost. For NA/NB, replace rear window at same time. Apply 303 Aerospace Protectant or RaggTopp UV treatment every 3-6 months to maximize top life.
symptoms: Visible cracks or tears in top material
Rear window yellowing, hazing, or separating from fabric
Water leaks into cabin during rain
Top material shrinking and pulling away from frame
Difficulty latching top due to shrinkage
